Animated characters who never speak word.Dug: A talker: in Up, his collar turns thoughts into speech, so he blurts out lines like 'I have just met you, and I love you.'

Whitney Houston songs.Greatest Love of All: George Benson recorded it first in 1977; Whitney's 1986 version went to number one in the US.
Whitney Houston songs.How Will I Know: The 1985 hit was reportedly written for Janet Jackson before Whitney recorded it, becoming her second number one.
Whitney Houston songs.I Have Nothing: From the 1992 film The Bodyguard, and an Oscar nominee for Best Original Song.
Whitney Houston songs.Run to You: Another Bodyguard track, a driving dance-pop number; the soundtrack sold over 40 million copies worldwide.
Whitney Houston songs.So Emotional: One of a record seven straight US number ones she scored from 1985 to 1988.
Whitney Houston songs.One Moment in Time: The 1988 Seoul Olympics theme, an anthem about seizing the one moment you get to shine.
Whitney Houston songs.My Love Is Your Love: The title track of her 1998 album, produced with Wyclef Jean and Rodney Jerkins.
Whitney Houston songs.Million Dollar Bill: A 2009 song from her comeback album I Look to You, her last studio album.
Whitney Houston songs.Queen of the Night: Dance-pop from The Bodyguard (1992), an album that became one of the best-selling soundtracks ever.
Whitney Houston songs.My Heart Will Go On: Celine Dion, 1997, from Titanic; a song that sounds like a Whitney power ballad but isn't.
Whitney Houston songs.Hero: Mariah Carey, 1993; Whitney's rival had a similar big voice, which makes this tempting.
Whitney Houston songs.Vision of Love: Mariah Carey's 1990 debut single, a number one; not Whitney.
Whitney Houston songs.Because You Loved Me: Celine Dion, 1996; a ballad written by Diane Warren, not Whitney.
Whitney Houston songs.Respect: Aretha Franklin, 1967; written by Otis Redding, who sang it first.
Whitney Houston songs.Natural Woman: Aretha Franklin, 1967; written by Carole King, Gerry Goffin and Jerry Wexler.
Whitney Houston songs.Halo: Beyoncé, 2008; a ballad in the Whitney tradition, but not hers.
Whitney Houston songs.Un-Break My Heart: Toni Braxton, 1996; written by Diane Warren.
Whitney Houston songs.Emotions: Mariah Carey, 1991; a similar powerhouse voice to Whitney's, but not hers.
Whitney Houston songs.Always Be My Baby: Mariah Carey, 1996; a smooth R&B ballad from Daydream, a different diva's catalog.
Whitney Houston songs.Think: Aretha Franklin, 1968; Franklin's cover of Think is famous from the Blues Brothers film.
Whitney Houston songs.I Will Survive: Gloria Gaynor's 1978 disco anthem, not Whitney.
Whitney Houston songs.Proud Mary: Tina Turner, 1971; Creedence Clearwater Revival wrote it first.
Whitney Houston songs.Believe: Cher, 1998; the first big pop hit to use Auto-Tune as an effect, not Whitney.
Whitney Houston songs.Fallin': Alicia Keys, 2001; a piano-driven R&B debut, not Whitney.

Bands with a number in their name.U2: Named for the U-2 spy plane, with the pun that the name also sounds like 'you too'; Bono has said the name was chosen for its ambiguity.
Bands with a number in their name.Maroon 5: The band went by Kara's Flowers as teenagers, and became Maroon 5 in 2001; Adam Levine's group scored its first big hit with Harder to Breathe.
Bands with a number in their name.Blink-182: The number has no meaning, and they started as Blink until an Irish band of that name forced the addition of 182.
Bands with a number in their name.Matchbox Twenty: Rob Thomas's Florida band sold over ten million copies in the US of its debut album, Yourself or Someone Like You.
Bands with a number in their name.Sum 41: They've said the name marks the 41st day of a long summer break when the band started, a number with no deeper meaning.
Bands with a number in their name.5 Seconds of Summer: This Australian pop-rock band's first three albums all debuted at number one in the US, an unusual feat for a new act.
Bands with a number in their name.Level 42: This British jazz-funk band took its name from the Hitchhiker's Guide, in which 42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything.
Bands with a number in their name.UB40: The name is from the British unemployment benefit form, Unemployment Benefit, Form 40, which the founding members had to fill out.
Bands with a number in their name.3 Doors Down: Brad Arnold has said he wrote Kryptonite in math class when he was a teenager, and it became their first hit in 2000.
Bands with a number in their name.The Jackson 5: Five brothers from Gary, Indiana, with Michael as the youngest; their first four singles all hit number one in the US.
Bands with a number in their name.The Four Tops: The Motown group kept the same four original members for over 40 years, an unusually long run for any band.
Bands with a number in their name.Three Dog Night: The name comes from the Australian outback, where a very cold night was a three-dog night: the number of dogs needed to stay warm.
Bands with a number in their name.Coldplay: No digits: Coldplay took its name from a university friend's band, who gave it away, and they were first called Starfish.
Bands with a number in their name.Queen: Queen's name was Freddie Mercury's idea, chosen for its regal sound and its bold, theatrical ring; no number anywhere.
Bands with a number in their name.Muse: Muse formed in Teignmouth, Devon; the name has no digits, and the trio built a stadium career on theatrical rock.
Bands with a number in their name.The Killers: The Las Vegas band took its name from a fictional band that appears in a New Order music video; no numerals.
Bands with a number in their name.Oasis: No number: the name came from the Oasis Leisure Centre in Swindon, which appeared on a poster of an Inspiral Carpets tour in the band's bedroom.
Bands with a number in their name.Nirvana: Nirvana is a Buddhist term for freedom from suffering; Kurt Cobain liked its idea of peace, not a number.
Bands with a number in their name.Genesis: Genesis formed at Charterhouse school and took its name from the Bible's first book; it never used a number.
Bands with a number in their name.Journey: No number: Journey got its name from a San Francisco radio contest; its hits have numbers in lyrics, but not the band's name.
Bands with a number in their name.Toto: Toto's studio musicians played on Michael Jackson's Thriller, but the name has no digit, just a short, punchy word.
Bands with a number in their name.Train: Train, from San Francisco, picked a word of travel; Hey, Soul Sister made them famous with a ukulele riff.
Bands with a number in their name.The Police: Sting's nickname came from a black-and-yellow striped sweater, and the band is a trio, so no number appears.
Bands with a number in their name.Duran Duran: Duran Duran took its name from Dr. Durand Durand, a villain in the 1968 sci-fi film Barbarella; no numerals.

Basketball terms.Slam dunk: The slam dunk was banned in college basketball for years, and some say the rule was a reaction to Lew Alcindor's dominance.
Basketball terms.Free throw: A free throw is an unguarded shot from the foul line, 15 feet from the hoop, and it is worth one point.
Basketball terms.Layup: A layup is a close-range shot off the backboard, and it's the first shot most players learn.
Basketball terms.Alley-oop: An alley-oop is a pass lobbed near the rim for a teammate to catch and score in mid-air.
Basketball terms.Three-pointer: A three-pointer was adopted by the NBA in 1979, and it transformed the sport into one of long-range shooting.
Basketball terms.Air ball: An air ball is a shot that touches nothing, and crowds like to chant the word at the shooter.
Basketball terms.Travelling: Travelling is taking too many steps without dribbling, and it is the most frequently called violation.
Basketball terms.Jump ball: A jump ball starts the game, with a referee tossing the ball between two players, though the rest of the game uses alternating possession.
Basketball terms.Fast break: A fast break is a quick attack before the defense sets, and it is the basis of high-scoring, up-tempo offense.
Basketball terms.Shot clock: The shot clock is 24 seconds in the NBA, and it was invented in 1954 to speed up a plodding game.
Basketball terms.Backboard: The backboard was introduced to keep fans from interfering with shots, and it is now made of tempered glass.
Basketball terms.Tip-off: A tip-off begins the game with a jump ball, a nod to Naismith's 1891 original, where the center jumped after every basket.
Basketball terms.Double dribble: A double dribble is dribbling with two hands, or after stopping and starting again, and it's a violation.
Basketball terms.Touchdown: Touchdown is football's, and basketball's highest-scoring game is Wilt Chamberlain's 100 points in 1962.
Basketball terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's, and basketball's long-range thrill is the half-court heave at the buzzer.
Basketball terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's target; a basketball hoop is a fixed 10 feet off the floor, whatever the level.
Basketball terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's, but Larry Bird of the Celtics won three straight MVP awards from 1984 to 1986.
Basketball terms.Puck: A puck is hockey's disc, while the NBA ball is about 29.5 inches around and inflated to roughly 8 psi.
Basketball terms.Scrum: A scrum is rugby's; in basketball, a tangle over a loose ball ends with a held ball and a jump ball call.
Basketball terms.Bunt: A bunt is baseball's soft tap; basketball's soft touch is the finger roll, a gentle layup.
Basketball terms.Icing: Icing is hockey's rule on shooting the puck down the rink; basketball's anti-stalling rule is the shot clock.
Basketball terms.Googly: A googly is cricket's spin trick; basketball's deceptions are the crossover and the euro step.
Basketball terms.Deuce: Deuce is tennis's 40-all, but in basketball slang a deuce is a two-point basket.
Basketball terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess; Naismith invented basketball in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets for goals.

Sports decided by judges' scores.Figure skating: Scores combine technical elements and program components. Judges grade each jump and spin, so a fall can erase gains from a hard jump.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Gymnastics: Gymnastics scores blend difficulty with execution, and a perfect 10 was once the cap. Nadia Comaneci scored the first perfect 10 at the 1976 Olympics.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Diving: Divers are judged on takeoff, flight and entry, and a tiny splash helps. Each dive has a difficulty rating that multiplies the scores.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Dressage: Riders guide the horse through movements that look effortless. Judges mark each one from 0 to 10 for precision and harmony.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Artistic swimming: Formerly synchronized swimming, it blends swimming, dance and gymnastics. Judges score technique and artistic impression, and swimmers can hold their breath for long stretches.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Snowboard halfpipe: Riders get scores for amplitude, difficulty, execution, variety and progression. The best runs fit big tricks into five or six hits.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Surfing: Surfers are scored 0 to 10 per wave on speed, power and flow, and the best two waves count toward the final score.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Skateboarding: Judges score runs and tricks for difficulty, originality and consistency. It debuted at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Breaking: Breaking, or breakdancing, debuted at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Judges evaluate technique, vocabulary, execution, musicality and originality in battles.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Trampoline: Gymnasts perform ten bounces without stopping, judged on execution, difficulty and time in the air.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Bodybuilding: Judges compare physiques for muscle size, symmetry and definition rather than lifting totals, so it's a sport scored on looks.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Sprinting: Sprints are decided by the clock and a photo finish, not opinions. Usain Bolt's 9.58 seconds for 100 m stands as the record.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Marathon: The marathon is won by whoever crosses the line first; the 42.195 km distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Rowing: Rowing races are decided at the finish line, and crews who reach it first win. No judges are required.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Cycling: Cycling results come from the clock or finish line, though in some track events, such as the omnium, points are tallied.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Soccer: Soccer has referees, but they enforce rules, not score style. The goals decide the winner.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Tennis: Tennis is decided by points won, not impressions, and electronic line calling now removes many human judgment calls.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Basketball: Baskets decide the winner. Referees enforce rules but don't score elegance.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Weightlifting: Lifts are measured in kilos on the bar, and the heaviest valid lift wins. Referees only decide whether the lift was legal.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Long jump: The winner is the longest measured jump, with no style marks. Mike Powell's 8.95 m from 1991 still stands as the world record.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Archery: Arrows score by ring: 10 in the center. It's measured on target, not judged.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Golf: Golf is the classic stroke count sport: the lowest total wins, whatever the style.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Speed skating: Speed skating is decided by the clock, and times are measured to the thousandth of a second.
Sports decided by judges' scores.Luge: Luge is won by timing, and sliders can top 140 km/h while lying on their backs.

Sports gear with wheels.Skateboard: Invented by California surfers in the 1950s who wanted something for flat-water days, it was once called sidewalk surfing.
Sports gear with wheels.Bicycle: The chain-driven safety bicycle of the 1880s let ordinary people ride, and it became a major force in women's independence.
Sports gear with wheels.BMX: Started in 1970s California when kids imitated motocross riders on bikes, and it became an Olympic sport in 2008.
Sports gear with wheels.Roller skates: The first inline-style skates were made in the 1760s by an inventor who famously crashed into a mirror at a party while playing violin.
Sports gear with wheels.Inline skates: Modern ones came from two Minnesota hockey players in 1980 who wanted to practise in summer, and they sold the brand Rollerblade.
Sports gear with wheels.Racing wheelchair: Built with a tilted, three-wheel frame, it lets racers exceed 30 km/h over a marathon, and top athletes finish in about 1 hour 20.
Sports gear with wheels.Go-kart: Built in 1956 by a California hot-rodder using lawn mower engines, and many Formula 1 drivers started their careers in it.
Sports gear with wheels.Scooter: A kick scooter became a craze in the early 2000s with folding aluminium models, and it's now widely used for stunts.
Sports gear with wheels.Unicycle: With just one wheel, it requires constant balance, and there's an official sport of unicycle hockey and mountain riding.
Sports gear with wheels.Soapbox car: Gravity-powered racers built by kids, and in America the All-American Soap Box Derby has run since 1934.
Sports gear with wheels.Longboard: A longer skateboard, designed for cruising, and its shape was copied from surfboards.
Sports gear with wheels.Penny-farthing: The giant front wheel gave speed before chains, and its name came from two British coins, one big and one small.
Sports gear with wheels.Sled: Slides on runners and not wheels, and in snow it's all about low friction.
Sports gear with wheels.Snowboard: Rides on snow with a flat base, no wheels, and the first mass-made one, the Snurfer, started as a toy in 1965.
Sports gear with wheels.Skis: Strapped to the feet, they glide on snow, and the oldest known skis are thousands of years old, from Russia and Scandinavia.
Sports gear with wheels.Surfboard: Rides on water, with a fin at the back for steering, and no wheels.
Sports gear with wheels.Bobsleigh: Steel sleds with runners, not wheels, so nothing here rolls.
Sports gear with wheels.Luge: A small sled using runners, so no wheels, and it hurtles down ice tracks.
Sports gear with wheels.Kayak: A paddled boat originally built by the Inuit from sealskin over a driftwood or bone frame, so definitely no wheels.
Sports gear with wheels.Ice skates: Blades glide on a thin film of water, and they don't have wheels.
Sports gear with wheels.Toboggan: A flat-bottomed sled on snow, with no wheels, and tobogganing was popular in Canada long before the word was borrowed.
Sports gear with wheels.Pogo stick: A spring-loaded pole you bounce on, with no wheels, and a patent from 1919 by a German inventor.
Sports gear with wheels.Stilts: Poles that raise you above the ground, with no wheels, and they have been used for crossing marshes.
Sports gear with wheels.Trampoline: Invented in 1930s Iowa by a gymnast and a diving coach, and it trains astronauts, but it has no wheels.

Moon gods and goddesses.Selene: The Greek moon goddess who rode a chariot across the night sky. She fell in love with the sleeping shepherd Endymion.
Moon gods and goddesses.Luna: Roman moon goddess, and the name gives us "lunar," "lunatic" and, from old belief, the moon's supposed effects on the mind.
Moon gods and goddesses.Diana: Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, equal to Artemis. Her temple at Ephesus was a wonder of the ancient world.
Moon gods and goddesses.Thoth: Egyptian god of wisdom, writing and the moon, shown as an ibis or baboon. He recorded the weighing of souls.
Moon gods and goddesses.Khonsu: The Egyptian moon god whose name means "traveler." He's often shown as a youth wearing the crescent moon and a sidelock.
Moon gods and goddesses.Mani: The Norse moon personified, who drives a chariot of the moon pursued by a wolf. His sister Sol drives the sun.
Moon gods and goddesses.Chang'e: The Chinese moon goddess, the star of the Mid-Autumn Festival's tales. China named its lunar probes after her.
Moon gods and goddesses.Tsukuyomi: Japanese god of the moon. He killed the food goddess in anger, and this caused his sister Amaterasu to refuse to look at him.
Moon gods and goddesses.Artemis: Greek goddess of the hunt, wild animals and, later, the moon. Her twin brother is Apollo.
Moon gods and goddesses.Helios: The Greek sun god, so the opposite of the moon, and drove a chariot across the day sky.
Moon gods and goddesses.Ra: The Egyptian sun god. Moon gods like Khonsu and Thoth are separate.
Moon gods and goddesses.Apollo: A trap: Apollo is tied to the sun in later tradition, and the moon belongs to his twin sister Artemis.
Moon gods and goddesses.Sol: The Roman sun god, the lunar Luna's counterpart.
Moon gods and goddesses.Amaterasu: Japan's sun goddess, not the moon. The moon is her brother Tsukuyomi.
Moon gods and goddesses.Surya: The Hindu sun god. The moon god there is Chandra.
Moon gods and goddesses.Inti: The Inca sun god, whose moon counterpart was Mama Quilla.
Moon gods and goddesses.Thor: Norse thunder god who wields Mjolnir and guards humankind. He rules storm and strength, not the moon.
Moon gods and goddesses.Zeus: King of the Greek gods and lord of the sky, not of the moon.
Moon gods and goddesses.Poseidon: Greek sea god, who shakes the earth, not the moon.
Moon gods and goddesses.Hera: Queen of the Greek gods, goddess of marriage, no moon duties.
Moon gods and goddesses.Odin: The one-eyed chief god of Norse myth. Not a moon deity.
Moon gods and goddesses.Ares: The Greek war god, hated even by his father Zeus. The moon belonged to Selene and Artemis, not him.
Moon gods and goddesses.Hermes: The Greek messenger god, quick on winged sandals, and guide of souls. He's not a moon god.
Moon gods and goddesses.Anubis: The jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming, not of the moon.

Mythical creatures (not real animals).Unicorn: Medieval writers took the narwhal's tusk for a unicorn horn and sold it for fortunes, so a real animal fed the myth.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Dragon: Fossils may have inspired dragon tales across cultures, yet no real animal breathes fire or has such wings.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Griffin: This lion-eagle hybrid has appeared in art since ancient Persia, and may have been inspired by Protoceratops fossils in Central Asia.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Phoenix: The firebird of Greek tales burned and rose from its own ashes every 500 years or so, and symbolized renewal in Rome.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Pegasus: Born from Medusa's blood when Perseus beheaded her, the winged horse later became a constellation.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Centaur: Greek myth portrays most centaurs as wild brutes; Chiron, who taught heroes like Achilles, was the wise exception.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Mermaid: Sailors, including Columbus, reported mermaids that were almost certainly manatees or dugongs.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Kraken: Norse sailors told of this sea monster big enough to be mistaken for an island; giant squid may be the seed of it.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Basilisk: Said to kill with a glance, this serpent king was hatched from a rooster's egg and defeated only by a weasel or mirror.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Chimera: A fire-breathing lion, goat and snake monster in Greek myth, slain by Bellerophon; in biology, a chimera is an organism with two sets of DNA.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Manticore: A Persian man-eater with a human face, lion body and scorpion tail; its name comes from a word meaning 'man-eater'.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Minotaur: Half man and half bull, it lived in the Labyrinth on Crete until Theseus killed it, guided by Ariadne's thread.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Narwhal: A trap: it's real. This Arctic whale's 'horn' is a tooth up to about 3 metres long, which spiraled out through its lip.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Komodo dragon: A trap: despite the name, it's real. The largest living lizard reaches roughly 3 metres and has venom glands.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Coelacanth: Thought extinct for about 66 million years until a living one was caught off South Africa in 1938.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Platypus: Scientists first thought it was a hoax: it's a real mammal that lays eggs, has a duck bill, and males have venomous spurs.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Okapi: This forest giraffe relative from Congo hid from science until 1901, and its striped legs help calves follow their mothers.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Giant squid: Real and enormous, up to about 12 metres, but first filmed alive in the deep sea only in 2004.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Dodo: A real flightless bird of Mauritius, gone within about 80 years of sailors arriving in the late 1500s.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Mammoth: Real and extinct: woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until roughly 4,000 years ago, after the pyramids were built.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Axolotl: A real Mexican salamander that keeps its larval gills for life and can regrow limbs and parts of its heart.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Pangolin: A real scaly mammal whose armor is made of keratin, like fingernails; pangolins are among the most trafficked animals.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Manatee: Real, and the likely source of mermaid sightings; this gentle sea cow's closest living relatives are elephants.
Mythical creatures (not real animals).Archaeopteryx: A real feathered dinosaur from about 150 million years ago, found in German limestone in 1861, soon after Darwin's book.

Famous castles.Neuschwanstein: Built from 1869 by Bavaria's King Ludwig II as a fairy-tale fantasy. Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle drew inspiration from it, though Ludwig died before finishing it.
Famous castles.Windsor Castle: The largest inhabited castle in the world and a royal home for nearly 1,000 years. A 1992 fire destroyed or damaged more than 100 rooms.
Famous castles.Edinburgh Castle: It sits on an extinct volcano and has stood guard over the city for centuries. The One O'Clock Gun is fired from it daily except on Sundays.
Famous castles.Bran Castle: In Transylvania, often marketed as Dracula's castle. Bram Stoker never visited it, and Vlad the Impaler had only a tenuous link to the place.
Famous castles.Himeji Castle: Japan's finest surviving castle, nicknamed White Heron for its gleaming walls. It survived wars, earthquakes and WWII bombing nearly intact.
Famous castles.Warwick Castle: A medieval stronghold in England on the River Avon, built by William the Conqueror in 1068. It now runs jousts and has a working trebuchet.
Famous castles.Prague Castle: The largest ancient castle complex in the world by area, according to Guinness, at about 70,000 square metres. It is the Czech president's office.
Famous castles.Conwy Castle: An Edward I fortress in North Wales from the 1280s, with eight massive towers. It was designed by Master James of St George, a leading castle builder.
Famous castles.Hohenzollern: Perched on a hilltop in southwestern Germany, it was ancestral home of the family that ruled Prussia and later the German Empire.
Famous castles.Balmoral: A Scottish estate bought by Queen Victoria's husband Albert in 1852. It remains a private royal home, and Elizabeth II died there in 2022.
Famous castles.Palace of Versailles: A palace, not a castle. Louis XIV turned a hunting lodge into this vast court of 700 rooms, with its famed Hall of Mirrors.
Famous castles.Buckingham Palace: The British monarch's London home, a palace rather than a fortress. It has 775 rooms and began as a townhouse of the Duke of Buckingham.
Famous castles.Westminster Abbey: A church where British monarchs are crowned and many buried. It has been the site of coronations since 1066.
Famous castles.Hagia Sophia: A 6th-century Byzantine cathedral in Istanbul, later a mosque, museum, then a mosque again. Its huge dome was a marvel of the age.
Famous castles.Notre-Dame: A Gothic cathedral in Paris begun in 1163. A fire in 2019 destroyed its roof and spire, and it reopened in late 2024.
Famous castles.Taj Mahal: A marble mausoleum built by Shah Jahan, a tomb and not a castle. Its inlaid designs use semi-precious stones.
Famous castles.Parthenon: An ancient Greek temple to Athena, not a fortress. It sat on the Acropolis and later served as a church, mosque and gunpowder store.
Famous castles.Colosseum: A Roman amphitheatre, not a castle. Over the centuries, locals quarried it for building stone.
Famous castles.Sistine Chapel: A Vatican chapel famous for Michelangelo's ceiling, painted between 1508 and 1512. It is also where cardinals elect a new pope.
Famous castles.Big Ben: Properly the great bell inside the clock tower at Westminster, not the tower itself. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Famous castles.Stonehenge: A prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain, thousands of years older than any castle. Some stones were hauled from Wales, about 240 km away.
Famous castles.Sagrada Familia: Gaudí's still-unfinished basilica in Barcelona, begun in 1882. It's a church with towering spires, not a castle.
Famous castles.Petra: A rock-cut city in Jordan, famous for the Treasury facade. It was a Nabataean trading capital, not a castle.
Famous castles.Pantheon: An ancient Roman temple that became a church, not a castle. Its dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever made.

Historic landmarks in the UK.Stonehenge: Neolithic and Bronze Age stones raised around 5,000 years ago. The huge sarsens came from nearby, but the smaller bluestones were hauled from Wales.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Tower of London: William the Conqueror began it after 1066, and the Crown Jewels are kept here. Its famous ravens are said to protect the kingdom.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Big Ben: The name actually belongs to the bell, not the tower, which was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012. The bell weighs about 13 tonnes.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Hadrian's Wall: Begun in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian, it marked the northern edge of Roman Britain and ran about 73 miles coast to coast.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Edinburgh Castle: It sits on an extinct volcano's rock. A one o'clock gun has fired from it daily, except Sundays, since 1861.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Westminster Abbey: Every English coronation since 1066 has been held here. Many monarchs, poets and Isaac Newton are buried within.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Windsor Castle: The oldest and largest inhabited castle in the world, in use by royalty for nearly a thousand years.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Buckingham Palace: The royal residence since 1837, with 775 rooms. Its famous balcony is where the royal family greets crowds.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Caernarfon Castle: Edward I built this Welsh fortress in the 1280s, and its polygonal towers were meant to echo Constantinople's walls. It later hosted the investiture of Princes of Wales.
Historic landmarks in the UK.St Paul's Cathedral: Christopher Wren designed it after the Great Fire of 1666. Its dome is among the largest in the world, and it survived the Blitz.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Tower Bridge: Often mistaken for London Bridge, this 1894 bridge has bascules that lift to let ships through, still operated today.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Avebury: A Neolithic stone circle in Wiltshire, larger than Stonehenge's, and large enough to hold a village inside it.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Eiffel Tower: Trap: this iron tower was built for the 1889 Paris World's Fair, so it belongs to France, not the UK. A common mix-up with London's landmarks.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Blarney Castle: Trap: an Irish castle where visitors kiss the Stone of Eloquence, said to grant the gift of gab.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Newgrange: Trap: an Irish passage tomb older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, famous for its winter solstice light show.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Mont-Saint-Michel: Trap: a tidal island abbey in Normandy, France. It sits just across the Channel, but it is French, not British.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Versailles: Trap: Louis XIV's palace near Paris, symbol of French absolute monarchy. Britain's royal palaces are quite different.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Neuschwanstein: Trap: a 19th-century Bavarian castle built for King Ludwig II. Its fairytale towers inspired Disney's castle, but it is in Germany.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Colosseum: Trap: Rome's great amphitheatre. Romans were in Britain too, but this one stands in Italy, not the UK.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Notre-Dame: Trap: a Gothic cathedral in Paris, not London. Westminster Abbey is the British counterpart.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Brandenburg Gate: Trap: Berlin's 18th-century neoclassical gate, once cut off by the Berlin Wall. It is a German landmark, not a British one.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Kronborg: Trap: the Danish castle in Helsingor, the setting Shakespeare used for Elsinore in Hamlet.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Bran Castle: Trap: a Romanian castle strongly associated with Dracula legends, though Vlad rarely lived there.
Historic landmarks in the UK.Rock of Cashel: Gothic Paris cathedral begun in 1163, it was damaged by fire in 2019 and reopened in 2024. A marvel of flying buttresses and gargoyles.

Things that count as bedding.Pillow: Ancient Egyptians used stone and wood headrests instead of soft pillows, and soft feather ones came much later.
Things that count as bedding.Duvet: 'Duvet' is French for down, the soft feathers originally stuffed inside, and the word spread widely in the 20th century.
Things that count as bedding.Fitted sheet: It's famously hard to fold, because the elasticated corners tuck inside each other and refuse to lie flat.
Things that count as bedding.Blanket: 'Blanket' likely comes from Old French 'blanchet', a white woolen cloth, so the word comes from its color.
Things that count as bedding.Pillowcase: Some pillowcases are 'Oxford' style, with a flange border around the edge that frames the pillow neatly.
Things that count as bedding.Comforter: A comforter is a thick, stitched and filled bed cover, usually sold as a single piece without a separate cover.
Things that count as bedding.Bedspread: A bedspread is the decorative top layer, traditionally draping all the way to the floor.
Things that count as bedding.Duvet cover: A cover is much easier to launder than the duvet inside, which is why many Europeans skip the top sheet.
Things that count as bedding.Flat sheet: A flat sheet sits between you and the blanket, keeping body oils off heavier bedding, so it's the part that gets washed.
Things that count as bedding.Quilt: 'Quilt' comes from Latin culcita, meaning a stuffed mattress or cushion, so the word really did start in bed.
Things that count as bedding.Rug: A floor covering, not bedding; the Pazyryk carpet, around 2,400 years old, is among the oldest rugs known.
Things that count as bedding.Curtain: A window covering rather than bedding, though heavy ones began as bed curtains to keep out drafts.
Things that count as bedding.Lampshade: Shades diffuse light and sit on lamps, not beds, even though lamp and bed both live in the bedroom.
Things that count as bedding.Doormat: A doormat catches dirt at the front door, far from the bed.
Things that count as bedding.Tablecloth: Table linen rather than bed linen, and tablecloths have been used since the Middle Ages to signal wealth.
Things that count as bedding.Bath towel: Retailers separate 'bed linen' from 'bath linen', so towels are in the bath category.
Things that count as bedding.Bath mat: A bath mat sits on the floor to catch drips, a different category from bedding.
Things that count as bedding.Napkin: Table linen, not bed linen; the word comes from old French nappe, meaning tablecloth.
Things that count as bedding.Placemat: Table linen, not bedding, though placemats and sheets share cotton in many cases.
Things that count as bedding.Apron: 'Apron' began as 'a napron', and over time 'a napron' shifted to 'an apron', a classic language slip.
Things that count as bedding.Shower curtain: It protects the bathroom floor from splashes, so it's bathroom textile, not bedding.
Things that count as bedding.Dishcloth: Kitchen cloth, not bedding; its job is wiping dishes and surfaces.
Things that count as bedding.Oven mitt: Oven mitts guard hands in the kitchen, not in the bedroom.
Things that count as bedding.Tea towel: Tea towels are kitchen linen, traditionally used to dry crockery, not bedding.

Things usually controlled by a remote.Television: The first TV remote, Zenith's Lazy Bones of 1950, was wired to the set, and wireless ones came later in 1955.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Garage door: Garage door remotes use radio signals, and modern ones change a code each press, so a thief can't just record and replay it.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Air conditioner: Most air conditioner remotes send infrared pulses, and you can see them flicker in a phone camera.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Toy car: Remote-control toy cars date back to the 1960s, and some hobby models can top 60 miles per hour.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Drone: Consumer drones are flown by radio remote, and many have a return-to-home function that brings them back if signal is lost.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Projector: A projector remote usually points at the sensor on the front or back, so it often works by bouncing off a screen.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Soundbar: Soundbars often use remote controls that work alongside the TV remote, and many can learn commands from it.
Things usually controlled by a remote.DVD player: DVD players started to spread in 1997, and their remote was usually the only way to reach menu options at first.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Set-top box: Set-top boxes receive cable or satellite signals, and their remotes often control the TV volume as well.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Electric gate: An electric gate opens at a push of a remote button, and many include a safety sensor to stop if something is in the way.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Toaster: No remote usually. A toaster is run by a lever and a timer, and it is meant to be watched.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Kettle: Kettles are normally controlled with a switch, since a remote would be risky around boiling water, though some smart models have an app.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Fridge: A fridge runs constantly on its own thermostat, and few people need a remote, though smart fridges can use an app.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Microwave: The microwave oven was reportedly invented after Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near radar equipment.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Blender: A blender has a power knob and buttons on the base, and a remote would be a poor match for a spinning blade.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Hair dryer: A hair dryer is hand held and switched on at the handle, so a remote would have no purpose.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Clothes iron: An iron is operated by hand, and safety shutoffs are built in rather than controlled from across the room.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Stapler: A stapler is a purely mechanical hand tool, with no electronics and no remote.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Desk lamp: Desk lamps usually have a switch on the lamp, though smart bulbs can be controlled with a remote or phone.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Coffee grinder: Grinders are typically operated with a button or dial, and the burr type crushes beans to an even size.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Electric toothbrush: An electric toothbrush has a switch on the handle, and some of the high end ones vibrate tens of thousands of times a minute.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Juicer: A juicer has a simple switch, and a slow masticating one squeezes juice at a low speed to reduce oxidation.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Waffle maker: Waffle makers are switched on by hand and watched until the indicator light shows the iron is ready.
Things usually controlled by a remote.Rice cooker: A rice cooker is a cleverly automatic device with no remote: it stops by sensing the temperature jump when water is gone.

Things you can fold up.Napkin: Napkin folding is an old art; in 1600s Europe, banquet napkins were pleated into swans, ships and even castles.
Things you can fold up.Towel: Folded towels are a hotel signature; some resorts twist them into elephants and swans for guests to find on the bed.
Things you can fold up.Folding chair: The folding chair is ancient: Egyptians and Romans used X-framed folding stools, and the Roman curule seat signaled rank.
Things you can fold up.Map: Paper maps fold along set creases; the Miura fold, devised by a Japanese astrophysicist, opens with a single pull.
Things you can fold up.Ironing board: Its legs scissor together so a board that stands waist high collapses to a flat panel that slides behind a door.
Things you can fold up.Umbrella: The folding umbrella has ribs that collapse like a hinged frame; the first pocket model appeared in the 1920s.
Things you can fold up.Stroller: Strollers once folded in two clumsy steps; the 1960s Maclaren umbrella stroller, built by an aircraft engineer, shrank to a slim cane.
Things you can fold up.Laptop: A laptop's hinge is its weakest mechanical point, and thousands of open-and-close cycles are tested before a model ships.
Things you can fold up.Deck chair: The deck chair takes its name from ocean liners, where passengers reclined in canvas chairs on the ship's deck.
Things you can fold up.Paper fan: The folding fan was invented in Japan, probably around the 600s, and later conquered Europe as a courtly accessory.
Things you can fold up.Bedsheet: A fitted sheet is the notoriously tricky one, but its elastic corners were a 1900s invention that stopped sheets from bunching.
Things you can fold up.Card table: A card table has folding legs and a top about 34 inches square, sized so four players can sit around it.
Things you can fold up.Brick: A fired brick is rigid ceramic; bend it and it snaps, which is why walls are built with stacked, not folded, units.
Things you can fold up.Mug: A mug is a rigid ceramic vessel; folding one would shatter it, though collapsible silicone cups do exist.
Things you can fold up.Spoon: A solid metal spoon doesn't fold, though camping versions have joints, and bent spoons were a famed stage trick.
Things you can fold up.Fridge: A fridge is a heavy insulated box with a compressor, which is not designed to collapse in any way.
Things you can fold up.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is a dense solid sphere, usually weighing between 6 and 16 pounds, so nothing about it folds.
Things you can fold up.Glass vase: Glass is a rigid solid at room temperature; bend a vase and it fractures instead of folding.
Things you can fold up.Candle: A candle is a solid wax cylinder; bend one and it cracks, though warm tapers can be gently curved.
Things you can fold up.Ceramic plate: Fired ceramic is brittle, so a plate cracks rather than folds; paper plates are the foldable cousins.
Things you can fold up.Light bulb: A bulb is a sealed glass shell, and the only thing that folds on it is the filament coil inside.
Things you can fold up.Pineapple: A pineapple is a solid fruit; each one is actually a cluster of dozens of fused flowers.
Things you can fold up.Doorknob: A doorknob is a solid fixed fixture, and a door's folding action belongs to the hinge, not the knob.
Things you can fold up.Bathtub: A bathtub is a heavy rigid basin, though inflatable and fold-flat bathtubs exist for travel.

Things protected by a PIN or password.Smartphone: Four-digit phone PINs have 10,000 possibilities, yet analyses of leaked codes show 1234 and 0000 are among the most common choices.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Debit card: The chip-and-PIN system was designed so a stolen card is useless without the code, and it sharply cut counterfeit card fraud.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Laptop: A laptop login password stops casual users, but unless the disk is encrypted, someone can still read the files by removing the drive.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Hotel safe: Many hotel safes let you set your own code, but most also have a master override that staff can use if you forget it.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Wi-Fi network: Routers ship with a default password printed on a sticker, and changing it matters because those defaults can follow known patterns.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Email account: Your email account is often the master key: 'forgot password' links for most other accounts get sent right there.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Burglar alarm: Many alarm systems have a duress code that looks like a normal disarm but silently alerts the monitoring company.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Tablet: Tablets can pair a short PIN with a fingerprint or face scan, and repeated wrong guesses can lock the device or erase it.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Voicemail: Voicemail boxes once had default PINs like 0000, and weak ones were exploited in the phone-hacking scandal at British tabloids.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Online banking: Banks usually add a one-time code on top of your password, because a single password alone is easy to steal or guess.
Things protected by a PIN or password.SIM card: A SIM can have its own PIN, and entering it wrong three times locks the card until you give a longer code called a PUK.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Toaster: A toaster has no secrets: its only control is a lever and a dial, and it is a classic example of a device that needs no security.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Fridge: Fridges generally have no lock at all, though some smart models connect to Wi-Fi, which means they do have passwords after all.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Library book: A library book is protected by a due date and a card number rather than any code, and that card number is basically the PIN.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Umbrella: Umbrellas have been around for about 3,000 years, first for shade in ancient China and Egypt, and nobody has ever needed a code for one.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Bus ticket: A bus ticket is protected by its printed code or barcode, which is scanned rather than typed, so there is no password to remember.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Coin: Coins are protected by nothing but their physical features; milled edges were added to stop people shaving off precious metal.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Receipt: Receipts carry no password, but they do often show the last four digits of your card, not the full number, as a safety measure.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Banknote: Banknotes defeat forgers with hidden features like watermarks, security threads, and color-shifting ink instead of any passwords.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Paper map: A paper map needs no password and no battery, and it still works in a place with no phone signal.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Notebook: A plain notebook has no lock, though diaries historically came with tiny brass locks that a hairpin could open.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Teddy bear: Teddy bears are named for US President Theodore Roosevelt, who famously refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a 1902 hunting trip.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Sofa: Sofas need no codes, but the word comes from the Arabic 'suffa', a raised bench, and sofas arrived in Europe via the Ottoman world.
Things protected by a PIN or password.Postcard: A postcard is the least private mail there is: anyone handling it can read the message, so it needs no password.

Things with prongs or tines.Fork: Forks arrived at European tables late; Catherine de Medici's court helped spread them in the 1500s, and many diners thought them silly.
Things with prongs or tines.Pitchfork: The farm tool has long tines for lifting hay, and the devil's pitchfork in cartoons is a mix of it with the trident.
Things with prongs or tines.Electric plug: The prongs are called pins or blades, and US plugs have two flat blades while British ones have three rectangular pins with a fuse inside.
Things with prongs or tines.Trident: Poseidon's three-pronged spear was a fishing tool, and Neptune carried it too, while a fisherman's version is called a leister.
Things with prongs or tines.Tuning fork: John Shore, a trumpeter, invented it in 1711, and a fork tuned to A vibrates at 440 hertz.
Things with prongs or tines.Garden fork: Gardeners use these to turn soil without cutting worms in half the way a spade can.
Things with prongs or tines.Carving fork: The long two-pronged fork steadies a roast so the carver's knife stays straight, and its guard protects the hand.
Things with prongs or tines.Rake: The tines on a rake are its prongs, and the rake gets its name from an Old English word for gathering.
Things with prongs or tines.Antlers: Antlers are bone that regrows each year, and a moose can grow a pair weighing up to about 20 kilograms.
Things with prongs or tines.Afro pick: The wide-toothed pick is thousands of years old; archaeologists found African combs in Kemet about 5,500 years old.
Things with prongs or tines.Spork: The spork combines spoon and fork, and its short tines fit a cup of soup or a plate of noodles.
Things with prongs or tines.Spoon: A spoon has a bowl but no prongs, and the word first meant a chip of wood in Old English.
Things with prongs or tines.Knife: Knives are blades, not prongs, though a knife and fork are the classic place-setting pair.
Things with prongs or tines.Ladle: A ladle is a deep scoop, and the long handle keeps your hand out of the steam.
Things with prongs or tines.Spatula: The name comes from Latin for a flat piece of wood, and its flat blade is made for flipping, not skewering.
Things with prongs or tines.Whisk: A whisk has loops of wire rather than separate prongs, and the shape is designed to beat air into eggs.
Things with prongs or tines.Chopsticks: These two sticks have no prongs, but they originated in China about 3,000 years ago and are used by over a billion people.
Things with prongs or tines.Scissors: Scissors have two blades, not prongs, and the pivoting design dates back to Bronze Age Egypt or earlier.
Things with prongs or tines.Hammer: The head has a striking face and a claw, but a claw is curved, not a set of tines.
Things with prongs or tines.Paintbrush: A paintbrush's bristles are too soft and too many to count as prongs, and the best ones are made from natural hair.
Things with prongs or tines.Toothbrush: Bristles are many tiny filaments, not a few rigid prongs, and bristle toothbrushes were first made in China in the 1400s.
Things with prongs or tines.Skewer: A skewer is a single spike, so one point is not prongs, though a double-pronged one holds food from spinning.
Things with prongs or tines.Spade: A spade has a flat blade for cutting soil, whereas a garden fork has the tines.
Things with prongs or tines.Rolling pin: A rolling pin has no prongs, though a docker with spikes does make holes in pastry.

Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Chocolate: Chocolate melts at around body temperature, so a hot car turns a bar into a puddle in a short time.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Crayons: Crayons are wax, and they soften and deform at around 50 Celsius or less, which a closed car easily reaches.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Dog: A dog can die in a hot car in minutes, as a car's interior can reach 50 Celsius or more in sunlight, even on a mild day.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Laptop: A laptop's battery can swell or fail in extreme heat, and manufacturers warn against leaving it in the car.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Lipstick: Lipstick is mostly wax and oil, so it softens and melts in the heat.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Aerosol can: Aerosol cans can burst when overheated, and the warning is printed on the label.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Smartphone: Smartphones may shut off or damage their batteries when too hot, as lithium cells hate extreme heat.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Candles: Candles will melt and lose their shape, and scented ones can lose their fragrance.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Ice cream: Ice cream melts quickly in the heat and loses its texture when it refreezes.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Medication: Many medications break down in the heat, so storing pills in the car glove box can make them weaker.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Vinyl records: Vinyl records can warp in the heat, and they can become unplayable.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Lighter: Lighters contain pressurized fuel, which in a hot car might leak or burst.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Umbrella: An umbrella is fine in a hot car, and you often need it in the boot anyway.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Spare tire: A spare tire is rubber built for road heat, so it survives just fine.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Floor mats: Floor mats are made to take heat and wear, and they can handle sun.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Ice scraper: An ice scraper is plastic and has no problem in the heat.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Jumper cables: Jumper cables are metal and rubber, built to stay in the car all year.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Road atlas: A road atlas is paper, and a hot car won't hurt it.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Tissue box: A tissue box is cardboard and paper, and heat doesn't bother it.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Seat cover: A seat cover is built to take the sun, and heat is no worry.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Car manual: A car manual is paper and lives in the glove box happily.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Snow brush: A snow brush is plastic, and winter gear survives summer fine.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Tow rope: A tow rope is tough nylon, and it can sit in a hot trunk without harm.
Things you shouldn't leave in a hot car.Windshield shade: A windshield shade is meant for hot cars, since it reflects sunlight and keeps the interior cooler.

Foods that contain fiber.Lentils: Cooked lentils offer about 15 grams of fiber per cup, over half of many adults' daily need.
Foods that contain fiber.Oatmeal: Oats contain beta-glucan, a soluble fiber linked to lowering cholesterol.
Foods that contain fiber.Chia seeds: Chia seeds absorb many times their weight in water and form a gel, and they are roughly a third fiber.
Foods that contain fiber.Black beans: Black beans bring about 15 grams of fiber per cooked cup, plus plenty of protein.
Foods that contain fiber.Raspberries: Raspberries are among the fiber-richest fruits, with about 8 grams in a cup.
Foods that contain fiber.Broccoli: Broccoli stems hold as much fiber as the florets, so peeling and eating them wastes nothing.
Foods that contain fiber.Pears: Pears with the skin on hold about 5 to 6 grams of fiber, much of it in the peel.
Foods that contain fiber.Bran flakes: Bran is the outer layer of wheat grains, which is why bran flakes are so fiber-dense.
Foods that contain fiber.Avocado: Avocado is a surprisingly good fiber source, roughly 10 grams in a whole fruit.
Foods that contain fiber.Popcorn: Popcorn is a whole grain, and three cups of air-popped hold about 3.5 grams of fiber.
Foods that contain fiber.Artichoke: A medium artichoke has around 7 grams of fiber and contains inulin, a prebiotic.
Foods that contain fiber.Almonds: Almonds provide about 3.5 grams of fiber per ounce, and most of it is in the skin.
Foods that contain fiber.Steak: Meat has no fiber; dietary fiber exists only in plants.
Foods that contain fiber.Eggs: Eggs contain zero fiber, as fiber comes only from plant foods.
Foods that contain fiber.Cheese: Cheese has no fiber, so dairy needs plants alongside it to supply any.
Foods that contain fiber.Milk: Milk has no fiber, despite being rich in other nutrients.
Foods that contain fiber.Butter: Butter is almost all fat, with no fiber at all.
Foods that contain fiber.Salmon: Salmon gives omega-3s but no fiber, because animal foods lack it.
Foods that contain fiber.Chicken: Chicken has no fiber; a chicken salad gets its fiber from the vegetables.
Foods that contain fiber.Shrimp: Shrimp shells contain chitin, a fiber-like polymer, but the meat you eat has none.
Foods that contain fiber.Water: Water has no fiber, though fiber needs water to keep things moving through the gut.
Foods that contain fiber.Olive oil: Pressing olives leaves the fiber behind in the pulp, so the oil has none.
Foods that contain fiber.White sugar: Refining cane or beets strips out everything but sucrose, fiber included.
Foods that contain fiber.Bacon: Bacon is cured pork, with only fat and protein and no fiber.

Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Lego brick: Lego bricks are made to tolerances of about two thousandths of a millimeter, so they're sturdy enough to hurt a lot.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Thumbtack: The thumbtack, in its modern form, was patented in 1900 by Edwin Moore, and it always lands point up.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Pinecone: Pinecones close when wet and open when dry, so their scales are hard and sharp underfoot either way.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Broken glass: Glass shards are hard to spot, and glass is made from melted sand, soda ash and limestone.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Cactus: Cactus spines are modified leaves, and they're designed to hurt.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Hot coal: Firewalkers get away with it because wood coals conduct heat poorly, though plenty still get burned.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Bee: Only female bees sting, and a honeybee often dies afterward because its barbed stinger gets stuck.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Rusty nail: Tetanus comes from bacteria in soil, not rust itself, but a nail can carry them deep into the foot.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Sea urchin: Sea urchin spines can break off under the skin, and the pain can last for days.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Thistle: Legend says Norse invaders stepped barefoot on thistles and cried out, saving Scotland, hence its national emblem.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Bottle cap: A bottle cap has 21 teeth around the crimped edge, a standard since William Painter's 1890s invention.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Carpet: Carpets hold dust mites and old crumbs, but underfoot they're one of the gentlest floors.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Grass: Walking barefoot on grass, sometimes called earthing, is popular, though the health claims lack strong proof.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Rug: The Pazyryk carpet from Siberia is about 2,500 years old, and rugs have been soft underfoot for ages.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Pillow: The oldest known pillows were stone ones in Mesopotamia around 7,000 years ago, which sounds painful.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Towel: Terry cloth is woven with loops that increase surface area, which is why towels absorb so much.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Moss: Moss has no true roots, which is why it feels velvety and surprisingly soft underfoot.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Bath mat: Bath mats make wet tile less slippery, and many bathroom falls happen while stepping out.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Yoga mat: Yoga mats are used barefoot because socks make you slip.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Fluffy slipper: A fluffy slipper is a shoe, so it's the one thing here that protects your feet from the rest.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Cotton ball: A cotton ball is nearly pure cellulose and almost weightless, so it's gentle underfoot.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Blanket: Blankets are among the oldest textiles; wool ones have been woven for thousands of years.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Feather: Feathers are among the lightest natural materials, and their structure is both strong and soft.
Ouch! Bad things to step on barefoot.Wet sand: Wet sand is firmer than dry sand, so beaches are easiest to walk on near the waterline.

Things that would make a terrible pillow.Cactus: Cactus spines are modified leaves that protect the plant from thirsty animals. Few things are less comfortable under your head.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Brick: A standard clay brick weighs around 2 to 3 kilograms, and it has been used in building for over 5,000 years. As a pillow, it is rock hard.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Pineapple: A pineapple isn't one fruit but many fused flowers, and its tough, spiky skin makes it a painful place for a head.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Anvil: Blacksmiths' anvils weigh dozens of kilograms and are made to take hammer blows, so one makes a hard, heavy pillow at best.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Cheese grater: A cheese grater has hundreds of sharp little holes made to shred food, and resting your face on one would shred you instead.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is hard, round, and heavy, up to about 7 kilograms, so it rolls away and gives no cushion at all.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Rubik's Cube: Hungarian professor Erno Rubik invented it in 1974 as a teaching tool; with 43 quintillion positions, solving it is easier than sleeping on its hard corners.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Cinder block: A cinder block is a hollow concrete building brick and weighs more than 10 kilograms, so it is a bad head rest.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Bag of nails: Nails are sharp metal and the bag shifts under your head. That is why it makes a fakir's pillow, not anyone's choice.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Pinecone: Pinecones are made of woody scales that open and close with humidity, and those scales would poke your cheek all night.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Toaster: A toaster is hard metal with a slot, and the lever and cord would dig into your head. It is neither soft nor safe.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Feathers: Goose down is among the best insulating materials known, trapping air in tiny clusters, and that's why high-end pillows use it.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Folded blanket: A folded blanket gives gentle support, and it's what many campers use when nothing else is around.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Teddy bear: The teddy bear is named after U.S. president Theodore Roosevelt, who in 1902 refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a hunting trip.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Beanbag: Beanbag cushions conform to your head and neck, because the beads shift, and so they support the head well.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Cushion: A cushion cannot match a proper pillow's shape, but its soft filling still gives plenty of comfort in a pinch.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Rolled towel: A rolled towel is a classic travel pillow substitute, and physiotherapists even recommend one under the neck for support.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Hoodie: A bundled-up hoodie makes a handy pillow, and you can also tuck your hands in the pocket. It is a trusted trick on planes.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Plush toy: Stuffed toys are filled with soft polyester fiber, so they squash comfortably under a head, which is why kids sleep on them.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Memory foam: NASA developed memory foam in the 1960s to cushion pilots; it softens with body heat and then slowly springs back.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Wool scarf: A wool scarf bunched up is soft and warm, so it is a good emergency pillow when traveling.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Duvet: A duvet is a soft quilt stuffed with down or fibers, and rolled up it makes a plush if bulky pillow.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Fleece jacket: Fleece is made from recycled plastic bottles in many cases, and a rolled-up jacket is a soft, warm pillow.
Things that would make a terrible pillow.Sleeping bag: Many sleeping bags come with a stuff sack, and campers often pack clothes inside it for an easy pillow.

Branches of engineering.Civil: Civil engineering is the oldest branch, and the name was invented to distinguish it from military engineering.
Branches of engineering.Mechanical: Mechanical engineering is among the broadest fields, covering everything from engines to refrigerators, and it grew out of the Industrial Revolution.
Branches of engineering.Electrical: Electrical engineering took off after Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla battled over direct versus alternating current in the 1880s.
Branches of engineering.Chemical: Chemical engineers design industrial processes, scaling a reaction from a flask to a factory producing tons of fuel or plastics.
Branches of engineering.Aerospace: Aerospace engineering covers both aircraft and spacecraft, and became its own field in the 1950s with the space race.
Branches of engineering.Software: The term software engineering was coined in 1968 at a NATO conference, in response to what people called the software crisis.
Branches of engineering.Biomedical: Biomedical engineers design pacemakers, artificial joints and imaging machines, bridging medicine and engineering.
Branches of engineering.Structural: Structural engineers calculate loads on bridges and buildings, a field that's learned from failures like the collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940.
Branches of engineering.Nuclear: Nuclear engineering began with the first controlled chain reaction in Chicago in 1942, and now includes power plants and ship reactors.
Branches of engineering.Environmental: Environmental engineers design systems to clean water and air, and their work greatly cut disease from contaminated water.
Branches of engineering.Marine: Marine engineers design and maintain ships and offshore structures, and the largest cargo ships' engines are as tall as a house.
Branches of engineering.Culinary: Culinary arts are about cooking, so they're an art, and unlike the engineering degrees there is no engineering professional involved.
Branches of engineering.Fine: Fine arts like painting and sculpture are made for beauty, not function, and the word fine means they're made for aesthetics.
Branches of engineering.Martial: Martial arts take their name from Mars, the Roman god of war, and they include judo, karate and many others.
Branches of engineering.Liberal: The liberal arts were the subjects fit for a free person in ancient times, such as grammar, logic and rhetoric.
Branches of engineering.Performing: Performing arts, like theater, dance and music, are live, and the audience is part of the event.
Branches of engineering.Visual: Visual arts cover things we look at, such as painting, photography and sculpture.
Branches of engineering.Dramatic: Dramatic arts refers to theater and acting, from the Greek drama, meaning action.
Branches of engineering.Decorative: Decorative arts are useful objects made beautiful, such as ceramics, furniture and textiles.
Branches of engineering.Graphic: Graphic arts include printmaking and design, and graphic comes from the Greek graphein, to write or draw.
Branches of engineering.Folk: Folk art is made by ordinary people in a community, like quilts and carvings, and not by trained academics.
Branches of engineering.Pop: Pop art arose in the 1950s with Andy Warhol and others, who made art from soup cans and comic strips.
Branches of engineering.Street: Street art started with graffiti and now includes murals, with Banksy as one of the best known names.
Branches of engineering.Abstract: Abstract art doesn't try to show reality. Wassily Kandinsky is often credited with painting one of the first purely abstract works around 1910.

Processors made by Intel or AMD.Pentium: Intel's 1993 chip got a name because numbers couldn't be trademarked; a 1994 floating-point bug cost it about $475 million.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Celeron: Intel's budget line, launched in 1998 as a cheaper alternative to its Pentium chips.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Core i7: Intel's high-end consumer line, introduced in 2008, brought the Core i3, i5 and i7 naming that people still use.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Xeon: Intel's chips for servers and workstations, which have carried that name since 1998.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Athlon: AMD's 1999 chip became the first x86 processor to reach 1 GHz, in 2000, beating Intel to the mark.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Ryzen: AMD's 2017 line revived the company's fortunes and put real competition back into the PC processor market.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Threadripper: AMD's high-core-count workstation chips, with some models packing dozens of cores for heavy workloads.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Opteron: AMD's 2003 server chip introduced 64-bit x86, a design Intel later adopted for its own processors.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Phenom: AMD's quad-core line from 2007, the chip family that came before Ryzen.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Atom: Intel's low-power chip for netbooks and small devices that appeared around 2008.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Snapdragon: A trap: it's Qualcomm's line of ARM-based chips for phones, so it's neither Intel nor AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Apple M1: Apple's own ARM-based silicon from 2020, which replaced Intel chips in Macs, so it's neither Intel nor AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Exynos: Samsung's line of phone chips, made by Samsung, not by Intel or AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Tensor: Google's chip for Pixel phones, first used in 2021 and developed with Samsung, so not Intel or AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.GeForce: A trap: it's Nvidia's graphics card brand, since AMD's rival line is Radeon, so it's not a CPU line from either company.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Kirin: Huawei's phone chip line, designed by its HiSilicon division, so it's not from Intel or AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Raspberry Pi: A tiny, cheap computer from a UK charity that uses Broadcom's ARM chips, not Intel or AMD silicon.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Arduino: An Italian-born microcontroller board usually built around Atmel chips, so it's not an Intel or AMD processor.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.A17 Bionic: Apple's chip in the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max in 2023, which is far from Intel or AMD territory.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Dimensity: MediaTek's mobile processor line for phones, which isn't from Intel or AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Tegra: Nvidia's system-on-chip line, which powers the Nintendo Switch, so it's not from Intel or AMD.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.PowerPC: IBM, Motorola and Apple's chips powered Macs until Apple switched to Intel in 2006, so they weren't Intel's.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Cell: Developed by Sony, Toshiba and IBM for the PlayStation 3, which made it a unusual multi-core design.
Processors made by Intel or AMD.Helio: MediaTek's mid-range phone chips, which aren't from Intel or AMD.

Food delivery apps.Uber Eats: Launched in 2014 as UberFresh, then renamed, it piggybacks on Uber's driver network in dozens of countries.
Food delivery apps.Grubhub: It began in 2004 in Chicago, and its name is a mash-up of the 'grub' for food and a 'hub' of restaurants.
Food delivery apps.Deliveroo: This London-founded company is known for riders with teal backpacks, and it left Germany and Spain after short stays.
Food delivery apps.Postmates: Uber bought it in 2020 for about $2.65 billion, and it was known for delivering almost anything, not just meals.
Food delivery apps.Just Eat: Born in Denmark in 2001, it let customers order from local takeaways online before smartphones existed.
Food delivery apps.Instacart: It delivers groceries from stores, so it counts, even though the shopping is done by a person on your behalf.
Food delivery apps.Seamless: Seamless started in New York in 1999 and merged with Grubhub in 2013, so it now runs under the same owner.
Food delivery apps.Zomato: This Indian company began as a restaurant-review site called Foodiebay before becoming a delivery giant.
Food delivery apps.Swiggy: Based in Bengaluru, it competes with Zomato and also delivers groceries in minutes in Indian cities.
Food delivery apps.Glovo: This Barcelona-founded app delivers across Europe, Africa and Asia, and its yellow-and-green couriers carry almost anything.
Food delivery apps.Lyft: It moves people, not food, since its core is rides, and it started in 2007 as a carpool service called Zimride.
Food delivery apps.Airbnb: Founded in 2008 after the founders rented out air mattresses in their San Francisco loft, it books stays, not meals.
Food delivery apps.Tinder: Its swipe gesture was designed so that picking a match felt like a game, and it is about people, not dinners.
Food delivery apps.Venmo: It moves money between friends, and in the US its public feed of emoji-filled payments surprised many privacy fans.
Food delivery apps.Spotify: This Swedish streaming service has more than 600 million users, and the closest it gets to food is its podcasts.
Food delivery apps.Waze: Its drivers report police and crashes in real time, and Google bought it for about $1 billion in 2013.
Food delivery apps.Duolingo: Its owl, Duo, has become a meme for relentless reminders, but it teaches languages rather than delivering meals.
Food delivery apps.Shazam: It names a song from a few seconds of audio, and Apple bought it in 2018.
Food delivery apps.Strava: This fitness app is known for its segments, where cyclists and runners compete for course records, not for delivery.
Food delivery apps.Calm: This meditation app sells sleep stories narrated by celebrities, which is as close to takeout as it gets.
Food delivery apps.Robinhood: It popularized zero-commission stock trades, and its name nods to the folk hero who takes from the rich.
Food delivery apps.Zillow: The home-listing site made its Zestimate tool famous, which estimates house values, not what is for dinner.
Food delivery apps.Expedia: This travel booking site began as a Microsoft division in 1996, and the closest it comes to delivery is flights.
