South Korean tech companies.LG: The name stood for Lucky-Goldstar, from the merger of a chemical firm and the maker of Korea's first radio.
South Korean tech companies.SK Hynix: A leading maker of memory chips, it is a key supplier of the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators.
South Korean tech companies.Naver: South Korea's dominant search engine, it also founded the chat app LINE, popular in Japan.
South Korean tech companies.Kakao: Its KakaoTalk is used by almost everyone in South Korea, often replacing the phone number as how people connect.
South Korean tech companies.Nexon: Known for MapleStory, the game company is a Korean gaming giant and also owns Dungeon and Fighter.
South Korean tech companies.Netmarble: A Korean mobile game maker with hit titles like Lineage 2 Revolution.
South Korean tech companies.Krafton: The creator of PUBG: Battlegrounds, which helped popularize battle royale games.
South Korean tech companies.NCSoft: A Seoul publisher of Lineage, one of the first major massively multiplayer games in Korea.
South Korean tech companies.Sony: Sony is Japanese, founded in Tokyo in 1946, so it is not Korean despite its rivalry with Samsung.
South Korean tech companies.Nintendo: Founded in 1889 in Kyoto as a playing-card maker, it is Japanese, not Korean.
South Korean tech companies.Huawei: A Chinese telecom company based in Shenzhen, so not Korean.
South Korean tech companies.Xiaomi: The Chinese company's name means 'millet', and it was founded in 2010.
South Korean tech companies.Lenovo: Lenovo is Chinese and took over IBM's PC business in 2005.
South Korean tech companies.Acer: A Taiwanese computer maker whose name is derived from the Latin 'acer', meaning sharp.
South Korean tech companies.Asus: Taiwanese, named from the word Pegasus with the first letters dropped, so it's not Korean.
South Korean tech companies.HTC: HTC, from Taiwan, released the first Android phone in 2008.
South Korean tech companies.Panasonic: Japanese electronics giant formerly called Matsushita, not Korean.
South Korean tech companies.Toshiba: Japan's Toshiba made early laptops, but it isn't a Korean company.
South Korean tech companies.Sharp: Sharp is a Japanese electronics company, now owned by Foxconn since 2016.
South Korean tech companies.Tencent: A Chinese internet giant, famous for WeChat, so not Korean.
South Korean tech companies.Alibaba: Chinese e-commerce firm Alibaba was founded in 1999 by Jack Ma.
South Korean tech companies.Foxconn: Foxconn is Taiwanese and is the largest assembler of iPhones.
South Korean tech companies.Nokia: Nokia is Finnish, and it began as a paper mill in 1865.

Famous poets.Emily Dickinson: She published only a handful of poems in her lifetime; her sister found nearly 1,800 after she died in 1886.
Famous poets.Walt Whitman: His one great book, Leaves of Grass, was revised and expanded across his whole life, starting from a self-published first edition in 1855.
Famous poets.Robert Frost: He won four Pulitzer Prizes and read at John F. Kennedy's 1961 inauguration, where sunlight on the page blinded him.
Famous poets.John Keats: He died of tuberculosis in Rome at 25, and his gravestone reads 'Here lies one whose name was writ in water.'
Famous poets.William Wordsworth: Poet Laureate from 1843, he wrote of daffodils in the Lake District, helped launch the Romantic movement with Coleridge.
Famous poets.Lord Byron: Romantic poet who swam the Hellespont and died in 1824 in Greece, helping its independence fight. His daughter was Ada Lovelace.
Famous poets.Percy Shelley: Romantic poet of 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind', and husband of Mary Shelley, who wrote Frankenstein; he drowned at 29.
Famous poets.Pablo Neruda: Chilean poet and diplomat who won the 1971 Nobel Prize; his Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair made him famous at 19.
Famous poets.Rumi: This 13th-century Persian mystic's poems are often cited among the most widely read in the United States today.
Famous poets.Seamus Heaney: Irish poet who won the 1995 Nobel Prize, known for writing about bogs, farm life and digging, which he compared to using a pen.
Famous poets.W. B. Yeats: Irish poet who won the 1923 Nobel Prize and wrote 'The Second Coming', with its line 'Things fall apart'.
Famous poets.T. S. Eliot: The Waste Land made him modernism's star; his playful Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats later became the musical Cats.
Famous poets.Jane Austen: A novelist, not a poet; her few youthful verses are minor curiosities next to Pride and Prejudice.
Famous poets.Charles Dickens: A novelist. Oliver Twist and Great Expectations were first published in installments, not as poems.
Famous poets.Agatha Christie: A crime novelist, though she did publish a poetry collection, The Road of Dreams, in 1924.
Famous poets.Stephen King: A horror and suspense novelist; The Shining and It made him a bestseller, though he has also published short stories and essays rather than verse.
Famous poets.J. K. Rowling: The Harry Potter author, a novelist; her first book was rejected by about a dozen publishers.
Famous poets.Leo Tolstoy: A Russian novelist of War and Peace and Anna Karenina; he also wrote moral fables, but verse was never his calling.
Famous poets.Mark Twain: A humorist and novelist behind Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, known for prose, travel writing and wit rather than poems.
Famous poets.Virginia Woolf: An English novelist and essayist, with Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse in flowing, poetic prose that still isn't verse.
Famous poets.George Orwell: Wrote Animal Farm and 1984, plus essays like 'Politics and the English Language'; his fame is as a novelist and essayist, not a poet.
Famous poets.Ernest Hemingway: He published some verse in his twenties, but his fame rests on novels like The Old Man and the Sea.
Famous poets.Arthur Miller: An American playwright of Death of a Salesman and The Crucible, once married to Marilyn Monroe; a dramatist rather than a poet.
Famous poets.Jules Verne: French novelist of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, one of the most translated authors ever.

American painters.Edward Hopper: Hopper's lonely urban scenes, like Nighthawks (1942), even inspired the house in Hitchcock's Psycho.
American painters.Norman Rockwell: He painted 323 covers for The Saturday Evening Post over 47 years, and his Freedom from Want is among his best known.
American painters.Grant Wood: American Gothic's models were his dentist and his sister, not a married couple. The house is in Eldon, Iowa.
American painters.Georgia O'Keeffe: A 2014 sale of her Jimson Weed painting for about $44 million was then a record for a woman artist.
American painters.Andy Warhol: Born Andrew Warhola in Pittsburgh to Slovak immigrants, he turned Campbell's soup cans into art in 1962.
American painters.Jackson Pollock: Born in Wyoming and raised in California, he's famous for his drip paintings, made by pouring paint on the floor.
American painters.Andrew Wyeth: His Christina's World shows a neighbor with a muscle disorder crawling across a field, painted in tempera.
American painters.Winslow Homer: He painted The Gulf Stream and seascapes, after working as an illustrator in the Civil War.
American painters.James Whistler: American-born, he lived in London, so he's easily mistaken for British. His best-known work is Whistler's Mother.
American painters.Mary Cassatt: Born in Pennsylvania, she spent most of her career in France, but she is American, and so fits.
American painters.Basquiat: He began as the graffiti artist "SAMO" in Manhattan, and a 1982 skull painting sold for about $110 million in 2017.
American painters.Bob Ross: The Joy of Painting host, who finished each canvas within a half-hour episode, from 1983 to 1994.
American painters.Frederic Remington: He painted and sculpted the Old West in works like the bronze Bronco Buster, defining its cowboy image.
American painters.J. M. W. Turner: A British landscape master, and his Fighting Temeraire was voted the nation's favorite painting in 2005.
American painters.John Constable: The English landscape painter of The Hay Wain, whose Suffolk scenes are very British, so he's not American.
American painters.David Hockney: Though British, he has lived in California for decades, which makes him a tempting trap, but he's from Bradford.
American painters.Lucian Freud: German-born, he became a British citizen in 1939, so he does not belong in the American group.
American painters.Francis Bacon: An Irish-born, British-based painter of screaming, distorted figures, so he's not American.
American painters.Frida Kahlo: A Mexican painter of vivid self-portraits, though she spent some time in the US, she isn't American.
American painters.Diego Rivera: A Mexican muralist who painted murals in Detroit and San Francisco, but he is not American.
American painters.Claude Monet: A French Impressionist, who painted his water lilies in Giverny, so he wasn't American, despite wide US fame.
American painters.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist best known for gold-flecked The Kiss, from Vienna and not from America.
American painters.Edvard Munch: A Norwegian painter, famous for The Scream, so he's not an American painter, whatever his US fame.
American painters.Marc Chagall: Born in Belarus, he lived in France and in the US during wartime exile, but isn't American.

Characters created by Jules Verne.Phileas Fogg: He bets £20,000 that he can circle the world in 80 days in Around the World in Eighty Days (1872).
Characters created by Jules Verne.Passepartout: His name means "goes everywhere" in French, and he is Fogg's resourceful valet.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Professor Aronnax: A French marine biologist, he narrates the voyage after being captured by Nemo aboard the Nautilus.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Ned Land: A Canadian harpooner who is Aronnax's companion, always trying to escape the Nautilus.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Professor Lidenbrock: A German professor who deciphers a runic note and leads the descent into an Icelandic volcano in Journey to the Center of the Earth.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Axel: Lidenbrock's nephew, who narrates the underground journey and is the more cautious of the two.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Inspector Fix: A Scotland Yard detective who is convinced Fogg robbed the Bank of England and chases him around the world.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Michael Strogoff: The Tsar's courier in Verne's 1876 adventure crosses Siberia to warn of a rebellion.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Conseil: Aronnax's devoted servant, whose obsession is classifying everything, from fish to species.
Characters created by Jules Verne.The Time Traveller: H. G. Wells's hero has no name; he travels to the far future in The Time Machine (1895).
Characters created by Jules Verne.Dr. Moreau: Wells's mad vivisectionist lives on an island, a different author's creation.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Allan Quatermain: Allan Quatermain is H. Rider Haggard's hunter-adventurer of King Solomon's Mines (1885).
Characters created by Jules Verne.Professor Challenger: Arthur Conan Doyle's explosive scientist leads the expedition in The Lost World (1912).
Characters created by Jules Verne.Robinson Crusoe: Daniel Defoe's castaway comes from a 1719 novel, not Verne's.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Gulliver: Swift's traveler visits Lilliput and Brobdingnag, not Verne's creation.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Captain Ahab: Melville's obsessed whaling captain chases Moby-Dick, written by an American in 1851.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Long John Silver: Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate with a parrot from Treasure Island (1883).
Characters created by Jules Verne.Baron Munchausen: Raspe's exaggerating baron is German and from 1785.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Sherlock Holmes: Doyle's detective lives at 221B Baker Street, not Verne's world.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Dr. Jekyll: Stevenson's split-personality doctor, from 1886, is not Verne's.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Dracula: Stoker's vampire count comes from 1897, not from Verne.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Edmond Dantès: Dumas's wronged sailor in The Count of Monte Cristo (1844) is French but not Verne's.
Characters created by Jules Verne.Tarzan: Edgar Rice Burroughs's ape-raised lord first appeared in 1912, an American creation rather than Verne's.

Bumpy things.Toad: A toad's warty look is mostly harmless lumps, though large glands behind its eyes can release a bitter, irritating poison.
Bumpy things.Pickle: A cucumber becomes a pickle after brining, and the bumps are tiny spines that older varieties often carried.
Bumpy things.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap began in 1957 as a failed textured wallpaper, before its inventors realized it was ideal packing.
Bumpy things.Lego brick: Lego studs are made to precise tolerances so bricks clutch together, and bricks from the 1960s still fit modern ones.
Bumpy things.Braille: Braille uses six-dot cells, invented by Louis Braille at age 15, and the dots are raised about half a millimeter.
Bumpy things.Hass avocado: The Hass avocado's bumpy skin darkens from green to near black as it ripens, and nearly all trace to one California tree.
Bumpy things.Bitter melon: Bitter melon has a warty, ridged skin and a bitterness that is prized in Asian and Caribbean cooking.
Bumpy things.Lychee: The lychee's rough pink-red shell peels away to reveal a juicy white fruit with a perfume-like scent.
Bumpy things.Crocodile skin: Crocodiles have bumps called integumentary sense organs that detect tiny pressure ripples in water, helping them sense prey.
Bumpy things.Speed bump: Speed bumps are widely credited to the 1950s, when a New Jersey inventor patented the idea; they now go by many names.
Bumpy things.Goosebumps: Goosebumps come from tiny muscles pulling hairs upright, a reflex that once fluffed our furry ancestors' coats for warmth.
Bumpy things.Rumble strip: Rumble strips are grooves cut into road edges that create a loud vibration to wake drifting drivers.
Bumpy things.Mirror: A mirror is made to be perfectly flat; any bumps would instantly warp the reflection.
Bumpy things.Window glass: Window glass is made by floating molten glass on liquid tin, which produces an extremely flat, smooth surface.
Bumpy things.Balloon: A balloon is stretched smooth by the air inside it, though lumpy rubber is visible when it is uninflated.
Bumpy things.Marble: Marbles are polished smooth and round, and they have been used in children's games for thousands of years.
Bumpy things.Egg: An eggshell feels smooth but is dotted with thousands of microscopic pores that let gases pass through.
Bumpy things.Ice rink: Rinks are resurfaced with a machine that shaves and floods the ice, leaving a smooth sheet for skaters.
Bumpy things.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is smooth except for the finger holes, and lanes are oiled so it glides rather than bounces.
Bumpy things.Pearl: Pearls are layered nacre smooth to the touch; irregular lumpy ones are called baroque pearls.
Bumpy things.Plum: A plum's skin is smooth with a waxy bloom, which is a natural protective coating you can wipe off.
Bumpy things.Silk sheet: Silk is smooth because its fibers are long continuous filaments, and a single cocoon can yield up to a kilometer of thread.
Bumpy things.Banana: A banana peel is mostly smooth, with ridges but no bumps, and it turns slippery when it becomes squashed.
Bumpy things.Soap bubble: A soap bubble is a smooth thin film of water between soap layers, and it pops in seconds as the water evaporates.

Things you can tie in a knot.Rope: Rope has been made for at least 30,000 years, and sailors have developed hundreds of knots for it, from bowline to sheepshank.
Things you can tie in a knot.Shoelace: Many people tie shoes as a granny knot, which slips; mirror-image loops make a square knot that stays tied far better.
Things you can tie in a knot.Necktie: The necktie descends from cloth worn by Croatian soldiers in the 1600s, and the word cravat comes from the French for Croat.
Things you can tie in a knot.Scarf: Hermès began making its silk carré scarves in 1937, and fans tie them in dozens of ways, from headbands to bag decorations.
Things you can tie in a knot.Cherry stem: Tying a cherry stem into a knot with your tongue is a classic party trick, often said to prove kissing skill, though no study backs it.
Things you can tie in a knot.Balloon: Latex balloons come from rubber tree sap, and the knot works because the stretchy neck squeezes itself shut.
Things you can tie in a knot.Garbage bag: The plastic garbage bag was invented in 1950 in Canada, and most people close them by knotting the top.
Things you can tie in a knot.Ribbon: Ribbon was historically a luxury trim, and tying a ribbon in a bow is the standard way to finish a gift.
Things you can tie in a knot.Thread: A single thread can be knotted to tie off sewing, and the Chinese art of knotting turns plain cord into elaborate decorations.
Things you can tie in a knot.Dental floss: Dental floss was first made from silk thread in the early 1800s, and nylon replaced it in the 1940s.
Things you can tie in a knot.Rubber band: Rubber bands were patented in 1845 in England, and you can tie two together with a simple knot when one is too short.
Things you can tie in a knot.Pencil: A pencil's lead is really graphite, and the rigid wooden body snaps long before it could bend into a knot.
Things you can tie in a knot.Brick: Bricks are fired clay, among the oldest manufactured building materials, and they're far too rigid to tie.
Things you can tie in a knot.Spoon: Spoons are rigid, so they can't be knotted, though Uri Geller made a career of apparently bending them.
Things you can tie in a knot.Chopstick: Chopsticks are rigid sticks that can't be tied, though some cultures tie them together to show a family bond.
Things you can tie in a knot.Book: A book is made of stiff, layered paper, so you can't knot it, but you can tie it shut with a string.
Things you can tie in a knot.Ruler: A ruler is a stiff strip meant to stay straight, so tying it in a knot would just snap it, unlike its flexible cousin, the measuring tape.
Things you can tie in a knot.Ice cube: An ice cube is a rigid solid, so it can't be knotted, though two cubes pressed together will fuse thanks to a thin film of melt water.
Things you can tie in a knot.Coin: Pressed-penny machines can squash a coin flat and stamp a design, but nobody can knot solid metal like a coin.
Things you can tie in a knot.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is hard resin or plastic, and a standard one weighs up to 16 pounds, so no knots.
Things you can tie in a knot.Carrot: Raw carrots snap when bent, and early cultivated ones were purple or yellow, as orange came later.
Things you can tie in a knot.Dinner plate: A dinner plate is rigid ceramic, so you can't tie it, but you can wrap a ribbon around it.
Things you can tie in a knot.Smartphone: A smartphone is a rigid glass and metal slab, so it can't be knotted, though some flexible displays are being tested.
Things you can tie in a knot.Popsicle stick: Popsicle sticks are flat wood strips that snap when bent hard, so they don't tie into knots.

City metro and subway systems.Tube: London's Underground opened in 1863 as the world's first, and its name comes from the narrow tube-shaped tunnels of the deep lines.
City metro and subway systems.Métro: Paris's system opened in 1900, and its entrances, many designed in Art Nouveau style by Hector Guimard, are protected landmarks.
City metro and subway systems.U-Bahn: Short for Untergrundbahn, the German-speaking systems in Berlin, Vienna and Munich share the same name.
City metro and subway systems.MTR: Hong Kong's rail network stands for Mass Transit Railway and is known for its punctual service and its Octopus card.
City metro and subway systems.BART: San Francisco's Bay Area Rapid Transit opened in 1972 and crosses beneath the bay in a tube.
City metro and subway systems.MARTA: Atlanta's Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority serves the city's airport directly.
City metro and subway systems.TTC: The Toronto Transit Commission runs the city's subway, buses and streetcars, and its streetcar network is one of the largest in North America.
City metro and subway systems.Subte: Buenos Aires' subway, short for subterráneo, opened in 1913 and is among the oldest in Latin America.
City metro and subway systems.MRT: Singapore's Mass Rapid Transit, begun in 1987, is known for being clean and for strict rules against eating or drinking on trains.
City metro and subway systems.Amtrak: The US national passenger railroad connects cities over long distances, which makes it intercity rather than a metro.
City metro and subway systems.Eurostar: This high-speed train runs between London and mainland Europe through the Channel Tunnel, so it isn't a city metro.
City metro and subway systems.TGV: France's high-speed train set a rail speed record of 574.8 km/h in 2007, but it links cities rather than within one.
City metro and subway systems.Shinkansen: Japan's bullet train began in 1964 with no passenger fatalities from crashes, but it's intercity, not a metro.
City metro and subway systems.ICE: Germany's InterCity Express is a high-speed national train, not an urban metro.
City metro and subway systems.Greyhound: This is a bus company known for long distance routes in the US, not a rail metro.
City metro and subway systems.Uber: A ride hailing app, not a rail system, even though it competes with metro trips.
City metro and subway systems.Via Rail: Canada's national passenger rail service connects cities, such as Toronto and Montreal, not within one.
City metro and subway systems.Thalys: This high-speed train linked Paris, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne until it merged into Eurostar in 2023.
City metro and subway systems.Acela: Amtrak's fast service runs between Boston, New York and Washington, and it's an intercity service.

Groundhog Day, the film.Phil Connors: Played by Bill Murray, the cynical weatherman relives one day over and over until he learns to care about other people.
Groundhog Day, the film.Rita: Rita is the producer played by Andie MacDowell, and Phil can only win her over by genuinely changing, not by cheating the loop.
Groundhog Day, the film.Ned Ryerson: The pushy insurance salesman Phil dodges, played by Stephen Tobolowsky, whose cheerful 'Bing!' became one of the film's most quoted lines.
Groundhog Day, the film.Larry: Chris Elliott plays Larry, the cameraman who travels with Phil and Rita to cover the groundhog ceremony.
Groundhog Day, the film.Punxsutawney: The Pennsylvania town that holds the Groundhog Day ceremony; the film itself was mostly shot in Woodstock, Illinois.
Groundhog Day, the film.Weatherman: Phil is a TV weatherman, an irony the film enjoys: he forecasts the weather for a living but cannot escape one repeating day.
Groundhog Day, the film.Time loop: The film never explains why the day repeats, which helped make it the model that later time-loop stories were measured against.
Groundhog Day, the film.Bill Murray: He plays Phil Connors; Murray and director Harold Ramis reportedly fell out during production and did not speak for years.
Groundhog Day, the film.Andie MacDowell: She plays Rita opposite Murray in what remains one of her best-known roles, alongside Four Weddings and a Funeral.
Groundhog Day, the film.Harold Ramis: The director and co-writer, who was also Egon Spengler in Ghostbusters; he and Murray made several comedies together.
Groundhog Day, the film.Ice sculpture: Late in the film Phil carves a likeness of Rita in ice, a hint at how many repeated days he has spent mastering new skills.
Groundhog Day, the film.Pennsylvania: The state of the real ceremony in Punxsutawney, where a groundhog named Phil has been 'forecasting' spring since 1887.
Groundhog Day, the film.Dan Aykroyd: Ghostbusters co-star of Murray and Ramis, but not in this film. The trio is so often paired that it is easy to assume he's in it.
Groundhog Day, the film.Chevy Chase: Chase was reportedly among the comedians considered for the lead, but the role went to Bill Murray.
Groundhog Day, the film.Meg Ryan: A rom-com star of that era, but Rita was played by Andie MacDowell, not Meg Ryan.
Groundhog Day, the film.Ohio: Wrong state: the ceremony is in Pennsylvania. Ohio does have its own groundhog, though, Buckeye Chuck of Marion.
Groundhog Day, the film.Vermont: Vermont is famous for snowy winters, but the film's setting and its groundhog are in western Pennsylvania.
Groundhog Day, the film.Florida: Phil's grumbling about the cold and snow would make no sense in Florida, which is not where the story happens.
Groundhog Day, the film.Dentist: Nobody in the story is a dentist; Phil is a weatherman, and Ned Ryerson sells insurance.
Groundhog Day, the film.Detective: There is no detective plot; the only mystery Phil investigates is how to escape his own repeating day.
Groundhog Day, the film.Lawyer: Ned Ryerson is the annoying insurance salesman, not a lawyer, and no legal storyline drives the film.
Groundhog Day, the film.Wiarton Willie: A real Canadian groundhog from Wiarton, Ontario, who also predicts spring on February 2, but the film is about Punxsutawney Phil.
Groundhog Day, the film.Staten Island Chuck: New York's own weather-forecasting groundhog lives at the Staten Island Zoo, but he does not feature in the film.
Groundhog Day, the film.Sandra Bullock: Not in the cast: Rita was played by Andie MacDowell. Bullock's big rom-com was While You Were Sleeping, in 1995.

Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Solar: Enough sunlight hits Earth in about an hour to cover humanity's yearly energy use, and solar is now among the cheapest sources of new power.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Wind: Modern turbine blades can be longer than a football field, and wind already supplies a big share of electricity in Denmark.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Hydroelectric: Dams provide the largest share of renewable electricity worldwide, with China's Three Gorges Dam the biggest power station of any type.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Geothermal: Iceland uses heat from underground to warm most of its homes and generate a good part of its electricity.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Tidal: The moon's pull drives it, so it is predictable years ahead, unlike wind or sun. France's Rance station has run since 1966.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Biomass: It is energy from burning plants or waste. It counts as renewable because new growth can absorb the carbon it releases.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Biofuel: Fuel made from crops or waste, such as ethanol from sugarcane. Brazil has run many cars on it for decades.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Wave power: Machines capture the up-and-down motion of ocean swells. The idea is old, but it is far less common than wind or solar.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Hydropower: People have used flowing water for power since ancient water wheels, and it remains the oldest renewable source.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Offshore wind: Turbines at sea catch stronger, steadier winds, and some floating ones are anchored in water too deep for fixed foundations.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Coal: It formed from ancient swamp plants over millions of years, so it is not renewable. It is the biggest source of CO2 from power.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Oil: Formed from ancient marine life over millions of years, it is finite. A barrel holds 42 US gallons, or about 159 litres.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Natural gas: It burns cleaner than coal, but it is still a fossil fuel. Its main ingredient is methane, a strong greenhouse gas.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Peat: Partly decayed plants in bogs, which regrow only about a millimetre a year, so for practical purposes peat is not renewable.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Diesel: It is refined from crude oil, so it is a fossil fuel. Rudolf Diesel's first engine was designed to run on peanut oil.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Petrol: Made from crude oil. Americans call it gasoline, shortened to gas, which confuses it with natural gas.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Propane: A fossil fuel byproduct of oil and gas processing, it turns into a liquid under moderate pressure, which is why it is stored in tanks.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Lignite: It is the lowest grade of coal, sometimes called brown coal, and burns less efficiently than harder coals.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Kerosene: Refined from crude oil, it fuels jet engines. Jet fuel is mostly a type of kerosene.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Shale gas: Natural gas trapped in rock and freed by fracking, it is a fossil fuel which transformed US energy supplies in the 2000s.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Anthracite: The hardest, highest-carbon coal, it burns hot and clean for a coal, but it is a fossil fuel.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Coke: Not the drink. This is coal baked without air, used mostly to smelt iron in blast furnaces, so it is fossil-derived.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Tar sands: Sand mixed with thick bitumen, mined in Alberta, Canada. Extracting oil from it takes much more energy than conventional drilling.
Renewable energy sources (not fossil fue.Butane: A fossil gas from oil and gas processing, it is the fuel in many lighters and camping stoves.
